question: explain your experience with Kafka
answer:
I worked with Kafka at BCBSA, in the member, coverage and claims interoperability services. I wrote the producer and consumer code on the application side: a backend service processes a change to a member, coverage, or claim, publishes an event, and a downstream consumer picks it up and applies the update. That kept the receiving services current without needing a synchronous call back to the source system for every change.

The domain events I worked with were centered on member, coverage and claims changes, tied into the Home Plan, Host Plan and BlueCard concepts we worked with. It let different services stay in sync with each other without tight coupling between them.

question: explain your project at marsh in detail
answer:
At Marsh I worked on M2 Broker, the engineering platform behind the Bluestream digital-insurance brand. It exposed reusable APIs and configurable experiences across different clients, carriers and insurance products, and Insure My Tesla was one concrete product built on top of it. Spring Boot formed the core backend API layer there, sitting behind an Apigee-managed edge that handled client authentication and OAuth2-facing controls, and my work sat inside that boundary.

My main hands-on work was building and updating Apache Camel routes for carrier integrations, along with the carrier-specific JSON mappings into the platform's common insurance model. I also contributed directly to the IMT-Germany analysis and documentation, working as a data modeler and system analyst on that piece, and I personally edited the architecture document for that effort.

That carrier-mapping and integration work is really what I'd point to as the core of what I built at Marsh.

question: how did you use Spring Security at NRG
answer:

question: tell me about your AWS Lambda work
answer:
My main hands-on AWS work at NRG was in 2025 with Lambda. I wrote Lambda functions along with their SAM templates and OpenAPI definitions, and I tested them locally with SAM against dev before they went further. I also helped push a domain-grouped module layout for the Lambda functions, working with a peer -- we initially leaned toward a fully fragmented design, but that created too many small modules and pipelines, so the team moved to a hybrid common-plus-domain structure once we saw the operational and build-management cost of the fragmented approach.

The wider platform had a lot of scale around it -- well over a hundred functions across a couple dozen module directories, with global defaults like a set memory and timeout, VPC attachment, and X-Ray tracing, plus a mixed cold-start strategy using SnapStart on most functions and provisioned concurrency on a smaller set of latency-sensitive ones. That estate-wide design wasn't something I personally selected; my depth was in writing and testing individual functions and shaping the module grouping, not in IAM, VPC, or deployment pipeline ownership -- those stayed with the lead and DevOps.

On the async side, I worked with SQS queues and dead-letter queues tied into the Lambda flows -- for example, JWT issuance enqueuing onto an account-mapping processing queue as part of token issuance -- and there was a scheduled Lambda-version cleanup job running weekly as a byproduct of publishing new versions on every deploy.

question: walk me through how you handled concurrency at NRG
answer:
At NRG the clearest concurrency work I did was on the dashboard's readProduct flow. It was calling out to several downstream services one after another - profile and contract data coming from SAP, plus offers, content, and Vivint flags - and that sequential chain was making the page slow. We parallelized those calls using CompletableFuture so they ran concurrently instead of one after another, and the load time dropped from several seconds down to roughly a second.

That said, I wouldn't describe it as a general concurrency strategy across the codebase. Async and parallel patterns like that were the exception, not the norm - most flows, including things like the DOD/Vivint-eligibility checks, stayed sequential and blocking. We reached for CompletableFuture specifically where a flow was fanning out to multiple slow downstream calls and the latency was visible to users, not as a default coding style.

Beyond that specific flow, I didn't build out a broader reactive or async story there - no WebClient or reactive stack, nothing like that. It was targeted: identify the slow fan-out call, parallelize it, verify the improvement, move on.

question: describe a technical disagreement and how you resolved it
answer:
The clearest technical disagreement I can walk through came up while I was building my own delivery platform, in the context of how a coding agent should decide what to trust when starting a new session.

The setup was that every fresh session was contractually required to read through several append-only state documents before starting any work, and those documents had grown stale and bloated over time — old queue items marked as still open when they'd been resolved, status sections that were months out of date, a lot of narrative that didn't actually answer what version was live, what was verified, or what was still open. The real disagreement was about which source should govern when the documents disagreed with what the repository actually showed.

I resolved it by writing a component that acts as a read-only view over those documents rather than a new document itself — it writes nothing, so it can never become another drifting source of truth. I built it to fail loudly instead of silently omitting anything, so a renamed heading or an unrecognized status causes it to exit non-zero rather than produce a summary that looks complete but isn't. And I set an explicit precedence order: real repository evidence outranks what the owner currently says, which outranks committed documents, which outranks old dated narrative.

That approach cut the mandatory startup context by over 90 percent without deleting any of the underlying history, and more importantly it settled the actual disagreement — instead of trusting whichever document was most recently written, the system now always defers to what the code itself shows.
